Title: Improving deep learning acoustic classifiers with contextual information for wildlife monitoring
Authors: Jeantet  L., Dufourq  E.
Focus: Focuses on improving the automatic detection of Hainan gibbon calls by classifying the presence or absence of their vocalizations using a multi-branch Convolutional Neural Network incorporating temporal information to reduce false positives
Significant Findings:
* For Hainan gibbon call detection, incorporating temporal information (time of recording) into a multi-branch CNN led to a 63% decrease in false positives on overnight recordings while maintaining high detection accuracy during daytime. Gibbon call detection also increased by 19%.
*Techniques from image processing, such as using geographical priors, can be effectively adapted for bioacoustics.
* Multi-branch CNNs offer a simpler approach to incorporating metadata compared to the geographical prior, although the geographical prior has advantages such as the ability to be trained independently and used with recordings lacking metadata.
* The described approaches can be adapted and applied to other calling species and use cases.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Investigate embedding methods applied directly to latitude and longitude metadata to learn geographical relationships. This could serve both for dimensionality reduction and to learn relationships between locations.
* Explore further modifications to the proposed networks to incorporate more prior knowledge about the environment and animals.
* Explore other types of metadata beyond location and time for different case studies.
* Further research into how to add contextual information can improve the generalisation of bioacoustics models.

Title: Ensemble deep learning and anomaly detection framework for automatic audio classification: Insights into deer vocalizations
Authors: Salem  S. I., Shirayama  S., Shimazaki  S., Oki  K.
Focus: Focuses on using machine learning and an anomaly detection framework to classify audio recordings for the presence or absence of deer vocalizations in two distinct Japanese environments.
Significant Findings: The ensemble approach, combining ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-B2, significantly enhanced classification performance, achieving 99.2% accuracy in the test stage.
Recommendations for Future Research:
◦ Hyperparameter optimisation.
◦ Exploration of alternative models, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformer-based models.
◦ Evaluation of the anomaly detection framework to ensure its accuracy.
◦ Validate the robustness of ML models across various hardware setups.

Title: Improving acoustic species identification using data augmentation within a deep learning framework
Authors: Macisaac  J., Newson  S., Ashton-Butt  A., Pearce  H., Milner  B.
Focus: Focuses on evaluating the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and data augmentation techniques for the acoustic classification of 18 small mammal species.
Significant Findings:
* Deeper CNNs improved accuracy, but this advantage diminished with larger datasets
* Sample quantity impacted accuracy more than network depth, with accuracy plateauing around 1600 samples per species
* Data augmentation significantly boosted performance with limited data (3.92-8.37% improvement with 100 samples)
* Novel samples outperformed augmented data; accuracy decreased when augmented data exceeded 50%
* Time shift augmentation yielded the best improvements, especially when combined with other methods
* Gaussian/background noise often reduced performance, particularly with poor signal-to-noise ratios
* Complex models like ResNet50 were more vulnerable to class imbalance; augmentation helped reduce errors for under-represented classes
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Investigate the optimal balance between novel and augmented data for various CNN architectures and dataset sizes.
* Explore the effectiveness of a wider range of data augmentation techniques specifically tailored for bioacoustics, beyond those tested.
* Investigate the impact of data augmentation on the generalisation ability of models to unseen data from different environmental conditions.
* Further research into strategies for handling unbalanced datasets beyond simply balancing using augmentation.
* Develop more sophisticated methods for selecting and combining augmentation techniques that are most relevant to the specific characteristics of different species' vocalisations.

Title: Passive acoustic monitoring of animal populations with transfer learning
Authors: Dufourq  E., Batist  C., Foquet  R., Durbach  I.
ML Algorithm Specific: DenseNet121; DenseNet169; DenseNet201; InceptionResNetV2; InceptionV3; MobileNetV2; ResNet101; ResNet101V2; ResNet152V2; ResNet50V2; VGG16; Xception
Focus: Focuses on using transfer learning to classify the presence or absence of the vocalizations of the Black-and-white Ruffed Lemur species using passive acoustic monitoring (PAM), especially when trained with a limited number of manually annotated call examples.
Significant Findings:
* Transfer learning with pre-trained CNNs is effective for passive acoustic monitoring even with very small datasets.
* For very small datasets, freezing the feature extractor of a pre-trained CNN often performs well.
* For larger datasets, fine-tuning the entire network generally yields better performance.
* ResNet101V2 and ResNet152V2 were identified as generally high-performing CNN architectures.
* Training on CPUs is feasible, making the approach more accessible.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Conduct additional experimentation on dealing with very small datasets.
* Explore the use of Siamese neural networks across various different species for very small datasets.

Title: Automated detection of Hainan gibbon calls for passive acoustic monitoring
Authors: Dufourq  E., Durbach  I., Hansford  J. P., Hoepfner  A., Ma  H. D., Bryant  J., Stender  C. S., Li  W. Y., Liu  Z. W., Chen  Q., Zhou  Z. L., Turvey  S. T.
Focus: Focuses on the development of an automated classifier using deep learning to detect the presence or absence of Hainan gibbon vocalizations in passive acoustic monitoring recording.
Significant Findings:
* The best performing model was a 2-D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that used spectrogram images (mel frequency scale) as input, and it achieved high accuracy in identifying gibbon calls. 
* Data augmentation significantly improved the model's specificity(reducing false positives by 79%) without negatively impacting sensitivity.
* The methodology developed in this study for the Hainan gibbon is general and can be easily extended to other calling species. The authors also provide accessible software notebooks to allow users to build and deploy their own acoustic classifiers.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Investigate the impact of environmental parameters and weather conditions on call detection.
* Explore acoustic spatial capture–recapture methods for abundance estimation in areas with suitable recorder placement.
* Develop classifiers to discriminate between groups or individuals for ecological insights.
* Determine call detection ranges under specific field conditions to optimise monitoring effectiveness and recorder placement.
* Expand and diversifying training data to further reduce error rates and improve generalisation.

Title: Automated detection of Bornean white-bearded gibbon (Hylobates albibarbis) vocalizations using an open-source framework for deep learning
Authors: Owens  A. F., Hockings  K. J., Imron  M. A., Madhusudhana  S., Mariaty, Setia  T. M., Sharma  M., Maimunah  S., Van Veen  F. J. F., Erb  W. M.
Focus: Focuses on the automated detection of the presence versus absence of Bornean white-bearded gibbon (Hylobates albibarbis) “great call” vocalizations within long-term acoustic datasets.
Significant Findings:
* The model greatly reduced analysis time, processing an hour of recordings in 19 seconds, compared to a minimum of 1 hour for a human observer​
* No significant difference was found in the temporal distribution of great call detections between the manual annotations and the model’s output​
* The post-processing stage significantly reduced repeated detections per call but did not eliminate them completely​
* The model struggled with low-quality calls
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Improve the post-processing stage to reduce repeated detections per call​
* Estimate call detection probability over distance to determine the effective area being sampled​
* Apply the model to long-term acoustic datasets across different habitats to analyze spatial and temporal variation in gibbon calling activity​
*Consider integrating hidden Markov models (HMMs) or recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the CNN to improve false-positive and false-negative rates​
* Extend testing to recordings from different locations to assess model generalizability beyond the study site​
* Explore alternative approaches requiring less training data, such as support vector machines (SVMs) or Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), for situations with limited datasets​

Title: There You Are! Automated Detection of Indris' Songs on Features Extracted from Passive Acoustic Recordings
Authors: Ravaglia  D., Ferrario  V., De Gregorio  C., Carugati  F., Raimondi  T., Cristiano  W., Torti  V., Von Hardenberg  A., Ratsimbazafy  J., Valente  D., Giacoma  C., Gamba  M.
Focus: Focuses on the automated detection of the presence or absence of Indri indri songs in passive acoustic recordings using a convolutional neural network (CNN).
Significant Findings:
* Data augmentation improved recall, prioritising the minimisation of missed songs. 
* Transfer learning generally enhanced accuracy, precision, and F1 score, particularly with new data.
* The model revealed the highest probability of indri songs during the warm rainy season and a peak in daily singing activity following sunrise, consistent with previous observations.

Title: ResNet-based bio-acoustics presence detection technology of Hainan gibbon calls
Authors: Ruan  W. D., Wu  K. Y., Chen  Q. C., Zhang  C. Y.
Focus: Focuses on developing an automated bio-acoustics presence detection network (BPDnet) for the passive monitoring of Hainan gibbon calls by classifying audio segments as either containing the presence or absence of their vocalizations.
Significant Findings:
* Proposed a ResNet-based bioacoustics presence detection network (BPDnet) for automated detection of Hainan gibbon calls.
* BPDnet significantly outperformed the baseline scheme of Dufourq et al. (2021) in bioacoustics presence detection accuracy, callback rate (recall), and F1-score by at least 12.9% when using the same test data and method without manual intervention.
* A fully automatic post-processing method based on the persistence of gibbon calls was proposed to replace the manual post-processing method in the baseline scheme.
* The proposed BPDnet with its automated post-processing exceeded the performance of the baseline scheme with manual post-processing in the same task.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Focus on improving the model's robustness to diverse acoustic environments.
* Improve the model's ability to detect weak gibbon calls that may not show complete features in the spectrogram. 
* Develop methods to distinguish strong breeze noise from gibbon calls to reduce false positives.
* Investigate the application of the BPDnet for the detection of other bioacoustic events or in different geographical locations.

Title: Automated classification of bat echolocation call recordings with artificial intelligence
Authors: Tabak  M. A., Murray  K. L., Reed  A. M., Lombardi  J. A., Bay  K. J.
Focus: Focuses on automating the classification of bat species from acoustic recordings using deep learning
Significant Findings:
* The model outperformed commercially available software, Kaleidoscope Pro (65% accuracy) and BCID (61% accuracy), on the same testing datasets.
* The study demonstrates that using plots of bat echolocation call pulses as input data for convolutional neural networks is an effective approach for automated species classification.
* The developed technology has potential applications in monitoring bat distribution and abundance.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Incorporate more training data, particularly for species with small sample sizes, such as the gray bat.
* Develop a model using higher resolution, full-spectrum acoustic data instead of just zero-cross data.
* Expand the training dataset to include more bat species to create a more generalizable model.

Title: A workflow for the automated detection and classification of female gibbon calls from long-term acoustic recordings
Authors: Clink  D. J., Kier  I., Ahmad  A. H., Klinck  H.
Focus: Focuses on a workflow for the automated detection and binary classification (presence/absence) of female Northern grey gibbon calls from long-term acoustic recordings
Significant Findings:
* SVM generally performed slightly better than random forest in terms of AUC and F1 score on the validation dataset.
* The temporal patterns of gibbon calling activity estimated by the automated system were not significantly different from those obtained through manual annotations of long-term spectral averages by a human observer.
* Applying unsupervised clustering to a reduced dataset of high-quality female calls that followed the species-specific structure suggested the presence of ten unique clusters. However, these clusters did not clearly correspond with individual female identity based on spatial distribution.
* The performance of this system exceeds that of some previously published automated detector/classifiers for primate calls but is below that of some deep learning approaches.
* The authors conclude that more work is needed before unsupervised approaches can be reliably used to estimate the number of individual animals occupying an area from PAM data.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Applying the developed methods across different sites and different gibbon species to determine the generalizability of the approach.
* Compare the proposed approach to deep learning approaches to assess the relative performance and requirements of each method.
* Develop approaches for predicting new individuals using PAM data.
* Explore different types of feature sets beyond Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs).
• Further tune and optimize of the RF algorithm, which was used with default settings.
* Investigate the performance of the proposed approach in other locations with different types of ambient noise.
* Explore the effect of recorder height on detection range.

Title: Bat2Web: A Framework for Real-Time Classification of Bat Species Echolocation Signals Using Audio Sensor Data
Authors: Mahbub  T., Bhagwagar  A., Chand  P., Zualkernan  I., Judas  J., Dghaym  D.
Focus: Focuses on developing a model to perform real-time classification of eight bat species echolocation signals.
Significant Findings:
* A compact CNN model achieved high bat species classification accuracy.
* The Bat2Web framework successfully integrated this model into a real-time, end-to-end bat monitoring system utilising LoRaWAN for data transmission to a web platform.
* Optimising the model for edge devices (TensorFlow Lite, TensorRT) resulted in slightly lower accuracy but increased F1-scores and reduced model size.
* The current model is specific to the eight studied UAE bat species.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Achieve generalisability to other bat species beyond the ones studied.
* Focus on developing a feature extractor for bat species to optimise various AI tasks.

Title: An Efficient Neural Network Design Incorporating Autoencoders for the Classification of Bat Echolocation Sounds
Authors: Alipek  S., Maelzer  M., Paumen  Y., Schauer-Weisshahn  H., Moll  J.
Focus: Focuses on classifying bat echolocation sounds at genus and species levels while differentiating them from background noise in acoustic data collected from wind test fields over multiple years.
Significant Findings:
* The proposed CNN-based approach achieved high classification accuracy for both bat genera (94.6% to 99.4% F1 score) and species (92.3% to 99.7% F1 score) on a previously unseen test set.
* Unsupervised learning using autoencoders and UMAP provided insights into data properties and helped understand the complex nature of noise recordings.
* Noise patterns varied significantly across locations and years, making their detection less robust compared to bat sounds when models were tested on data from different distributions.
* Classifier performance was influenced by the location and time of recordings, highlighting the impact of environmental factors.
* With sufficient data from various locations and years, the proposed model could effectively learn and classify bat sounds at both genus and species levels.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Expand the bat sound recording database by integrating data from diverse sources and locations.
* Incorporate habitat information to enhance the understanding and classification of bat sounds.
* Integrate video tracking with acoustic monitoring for a more understanding of bat activity.

Title: Development of a species identification system of Japanese bats from echolocation calls using convolutional neural networks
Authors: Kobayashi  K., Masuda  K., Haga  C., Matsui  T., Fukui  D., Machimura  T.
Focus: Focuses on the development of a bat species identification system for Japanese bats by analyzing their echolocation calls.
Significant Findings:
* This approach outperformed previous studies that attempted to identify a similar number of bat species.
* Guided Grad-CAM visualisation revealed that the CNN effectively learned to extract relevant features from the spectrograms, including different call types within the same species.
* The study highlighted challenges related to noise treatment, as overlapping frequencies between some bat calls and noise led to errors.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Change the deep learning algorithm from image classification to object detection. This could allow for the detection of the location of bat echolocation calls within spectrograms and simultaneous species identification.
* Apply the classifier to unknown bat echolocation calls to assess its feasibility for estimating bat fauna and spatial activity distribution.
* Explore the use of a lighter weight model structure to reduce the training time.
*  Standardize the recording protocol for sound files to avoid issues like accidental recording of multiple loops, which could overestimate performance.
* Include geographical information, such as habitat distribution maps, as additional features.
* Further enhance generalization performance by augmenting sound data with acoustic white noise, anthropogenic sounds, and insect sounds to better simulate natural environments.

Title: Bioacoustic classification of a small dataset of mammalian vocalisations using deep learning
Authors: Manriquez  P. R., Kotz  S. A., Ravignani  A., de Boer  B.
Focus: Focuses on the bioacoustic classification of affective vocalisations from a small dataset of four mammalian species: human infants, dogs, chimpanzees, and tree shrews, and evaluates their ability to generalise affective call qualities across these taxa.
Significant Findings:
* Transfer Learning significantly improved classification accuracy compared to training networks from scratch. Without transfer learning, accuracy was around chance level.
• Data Augmentation (pitch shifting and adding noise) also boosted classification accuracy in the small dataset. Combining domain-general (noise) and domain-specific (pitch shift) transformations generally yielded the best results.
* Among the tested networks, ResNet and VGG16 achieved the best overall performance, outperforming VGGish.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Future research should consider a more extensive range of species vocalisations to achieve more meaningful and robust results regarding different Data Augmentation approaches and their limitations.
* Incorporate additional acoustic parameters like MFCC and kurtosis in statistical analyses to better understand the differences between affective vocalisations.

Title: Deep-learning-based central African primate species classification with MixUp and SpecAugment
Authors: Pellegrini  T., Int Speech Commun  Assoc
Focus: Focuses on the automatic classification of audio recordings into four specific primate species (chimpanzees, mandrills, red-capped mangabeys, and guenons)  as well as a background noise category.
Significant Findings:
* The study successfully classified central African primate species vocalizations using deep learning.
* The best performing model was a standard 10-layer CNN (CNN10-16k), which achieved a 93.6% Unweighted Average Recall (UAR) on the development set and 92.5% UAR on the test set. This outperformed an official baseline of 86.6% UAR.
* Data augmentation techniques, specifically SpecAugment and MixUp, were very useful and brought significant performance gains. Using both together yielded the best results for the models tested.
* Using a balanced data sampler during training was generally more effective than a random sampler, especially for ResNet22, likely due to the imbalanced nature of the dataset.
* Applying an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the model weights resulted in slight further improvements in performance across architectures.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Try a hierarchical system to address confusions between the background class and primate species. 
* Train a single model on both objectives simultaneously, potentially using a multi-task learning approach, to better discriminate between background and the different primate species.

Title: A Deep and Recurrent Architecture for Primate Vocalization Classification
Authors: Müller  R., Illium  S., Linnhoff-Popien  C., Int Speech Commun  Assoc
Focus: Focuses on the classification of vocalizations from multiple primate species, specifically chimpanzees, guenons, mandrills, and redcaps, along with background noises.
Significant Findings:
* The proposed deep and recurrent architecture outperforms the best baseline methods on a recently published dataset. The best baseline, an ensemble of various deep and shallow classifiers, achieved a Unweighted Average Recall (UAR) of 87.5% on the test set, while the proposed approach achieved 89.3% UAR using an ensemble of the five best models found during hyperparameter optimization.
* The ensemble of the top five models achieved the best performance compared to individual models found during hyperparameter optimization, demonstrating the benefit of combining diverse models through majority voting.
* Redcap vocalizations were the most difficult to classify, potentially due to a lower signal-to-noise ratio in the recordings.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Investigate upon more sophisticated variants of pooling operations.
* Incorporate background noise removal tools to address confusion with distant vocalizations.
* Investigate upon the effects of pre-training the network with auxiliary data from various domains.

Title: Identifying Distinguishing Acoustic Features in Felid Vocalizations Based on Call Type and Species Classification
Authors: Bandara  D., Exantus  K., Navarro-Martinez  C., Patterson  M., Byun  A.
Focus: Focuses on developing a machine learning-based approach to identify acoustic features that distinguish felid call types and species within the Pantherinae subfamily
Significant Findings:
* The study identified duration, mean mel spectrogram, frequency range, and amplitude range as among the most distinguishing acoustic features for both call and species classifications
* The developed methodology provides an automated and non-biased approach for identifying key acoustic features without direct human analysis
* The research demonstrates that amplitude, time, and frequency-based features show significant variation between call types and species
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Perform additional evolutionary acoustic analysis using the interpretable acoustic features identified.
* Investigate the potential usefulness of the extracted features in future vocalization studies.
* Expand the application of the automated methodology for feature identification to larger datasets from long-term vocalization studies.
* Address the limitation of requiring a priori defined call types and species by exploring unsupervised methods such as autoencoders or principal component analysis to learn differences in an unsupervised manner.
* Continue to build and standardize datasets of felid calls from heterogeneous sources.
* Improve data collection to potentially track individual animals and avoid data leakage between training and test sets.

Title: DCNN for Pig Vocalization and Non-Vocalization Classification: Evaluate Model Robustness with New Data
Authors: Pann  V., Kwon  K. S., Kim  B., Jang  D. H., Kim  J. B.
Preprocessing Methods: Noise Reduction , Segmentation, Normalization, Feature Extraction, Augmentation
Focus: Focuses on the development of a model for the classification of presence/absence of pig vocalization in real pig farm environments.
Significant Findings:
* A novel audio feature extraction method called Mixed-MMCT, which combines Mel-spectrogram, MFCC, Chroma, and Tonnetz features, was proposed
* Mixed-MMCT achieved the highest classification accuracy on all three pig farm datasets
* The study concludes that combining multiple feature extraction methods, as done in Mixed-MMCT, improves the model performance for classifying pig vocalization and non-vocalization 
* The findings suggest that the proposed approach can be a significant and useful solution for automating pig vocalization data collection
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Consider pig vocalization classifications such as screaming, grunting, squealing, and coughing.
* Provide solutions for improving animal welfare monitoring in pig farms.
* Utilize the findings in this study for automating data collection to separate pig vocalization and non-vocalization for future work.
* Compare the performance of the proposed model with existing models (although a lack of a public benchmark dataset currently limits this).
* Conduct more experiments with existing datasets to further prove the model's effectiveness.

Title: Computer Audition for Continuous Rainforest Occupancy Monitoring: The Case of Bornean Gibbons' Call Detection
Authors: Tzirakis  P., Shiarella  A., Ewers  R., Schuller  B. W., Int Speech Commun  Assoc
Preprocessing Methods: Noise Reduction , Normalization, Augmentation, Feature Extraction, Segmentation
Focus: Focuses on vocalization presence/absence classification for the detection of Bornean gibbon calls using audio data collected by autonomous recording units.
Significant Findings:
* The proposed deep convolutional recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture significantly outperformed two other audio analysis toolkits, End2You and openXBOW, in terms of Unweighted Average Recall (UAR) on both the validation and test sets
* This can reduce human data processing times and facilitate continuous primate occupancy monitoring
* The developed audio annotation and extraction pipeline can be adapted to train bespoke call detection systems for other species and study sites
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Incorporate additional species in their workflow.
* Train their model to simultaneously detect and predict animal sounds.
* Release the data within a gibbon call detection Interspeech challenge event.
* Use transfer learning methods, which can be helpful when using small datasets.
* Apply the image feature extraction abilities of a model like VGGNet to spectrogram features, and then feed those features to recurrent components.

Title: Towards Automated Detection and Localization of Red Deer Cervus elaphus Using Passive Acoustic Sensors during the Rut
Authors: Avots  E., Vecvanags  A., Filipovs  J., Brauns  A., Skudrins  G., Done  G., Ozolins  J., Anbarjafari  G., Jakovels  D.
Preprocessing Methods: Noise Reduction , Segmentation, Normalization, Augmentation, Band-pass Filtering, Feature Extraction
Focus: Focuses on the automated detection, classifying presence/absence of red deer vocalizations during their rutting period using passive acoustic sensors.
Significant Findings:
* The study proposed and demonstrated a concept for an automated data processing workflow for the detection and localization of red deer stags during the rut
* Linear support vector machine (SVM) demonstrated the best performance with a detection accuracy of 96.46%
* A novel automated approach based on cross-correlation and spectral feature similarity was proposed for precise sound delay assessment in multiple microphones
* Spectral 2 stage approach, outperformed manual sound delay assessment by a human expert
* Acoustic recorders with GPS time synchronization could be effectively used to track red deer stag activities during the rutting season with the aid of automated data analysis
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Test the proposed localization approach on red deer calls with known source locations.
* Perform controlled tests with artificially created or recorded and played red deer calls.
* Evaluate the impact of wind (direction and speed) on detection and localization performance.
* Investigate the influence of reflection and reverberation of sound waves from vegetation and topographic relief on localization accuracy.
* Include the impact of wind and obstacles in the scope of future research.
Foster the uptake of passive acoustic monitoring using the proposed automated data processing workflow in red deer rut monitoring and for other animal species.
* Provide a more detailed insight into the rut of red deer using the developed techniques.
* Apply the proposed techniques for detection and localization of target animal sounds to other animal species.

Title: Classification of Elephant Sounds Using Parallel Convolutional Neural Network
Authors: Leonid  T. T., Jayaparvathy  R.
Focus: Focuses on classifying elephant vocalization presence/absence from audio samples using a parallel convolutional neural network.
Significant Findings:
* The proposed methodology achieved a better performance with an accuracy of 0.962 compared to the simple CNN  
* The proposed method also demonstrated a reduced computation time for the best-performing feature combination  
* MFCC + LPC showed better performance than other combinations in the simple CNN, while the proposed CNN also showed improved performance with this combination compared to some other combinations
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Explore the scope for further research in the methodology of parallel computing.
* Use different deep learning models in the classification process in future extensions of this work.

Title: An integrated passive acoustic monitoring and deep learning pipeline for black-and-white ruffed lemurs (Varecia variegata) in Ranomafana National Park, Madagascar
Authors: Batist  C. H., Dufourq  E., Jeantet  L., Razafindraibe  M. N., Randriamanantena  F., Baden  A. L.
Preprocessing Methods: Segmentation, Low-Pass Filter, Normalization, Feature Extraction
Focus: Focuses on developing a machine learning pipeline for the automated presence/absence classification of black-and-white ruffed lemur vocalizations from passive acoustic monitoring data.
Significant Findings:
* PAM outperformed in-person observations, detecting more calls   
* Using PAM, the study provided the first published evidence of nocturnal calling in black-and-white ruffed lemurs   
* The developed deep learning pipeline significantly reduced the time needed for data analysis  
* the potential of PAM combined with deep learning as a powerful and cost-efficient tool for biodiversity monitoring  
* An open-source graphic user interface (GUI) was developed to facilitate the use of the model for lemur vocalisation detection
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Statistically test vocal activity patterns in future studies, moving beyond qualitative results.
* Conduct future research in ruffed lemur mating behaviour and communication to build upon the preliminary results regarding vocal activity during this period.
* Use one type of recorder for future studies to mitigate inherent variation based on differing technical specifications.
* Consider and account for mitigating circumstances when selecting optimal deployment sites to minimise background noise and maximise detection range.
* Conduct more standardised experiments, such as playbacks, with multiple on-the-ground groups to better ground-truth and compare call detection by PAM and in-person observations.

Title: A Deep Learning-Based Coyote Detection System Using Audio Data
Authors: Jung  H., Kwon  B., Kim  Y., Lee  Y., Park  J., Pegg  G., Wang  Y. Q., Smith  A. H.
Focus: Focuses on the presence/absence classification of coyotes based on their howling sounds
Significant Findings:
* MFCC + CNN is the most effective combination for detecting coyote howling sounds.
* Audio-based classification is preferred over image-based for real-time, resource-efficient systems (e.g., on Raspberry Pi).
* The proposed model enables accurate, low-cost, and fast detection of coyotes to help prevent damage to livestock and property.
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Incorporate real-world environmental noise (e.g., wind, sirens, vehicles) into training data to improve model robustness.
* Develop a noise-tolerant dataset that maintains accuracy under natural outdoor conditions.
* Enhance model generalization for diverse acoustic environments.
* Explore better preprocessing methods for mixed or noisy audio clips.

Title: Using the BirdNET algorithm to identify wolves, coyotes, and potentially their interactions in a large audio dataset
Authors: Sossover  D., Burrows  K., Kahl  S., Wood  C. M.
Focus: Focuses on evaluating the BirdNET algorithm's ability to identify wolves and coyotes in a large passive acoustic monitoring dataset.
Significant Findings:
* BirdNET can be used to identify both gray wolves and coyotes in passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) data
* For coyotes in the northern Sierra Nevada dataset, BirdNET showed high recall and precision
* For wolves in the northern Sierra Nevada dataset, real-world precision was low, but recall was high
* Careful post-processing of BirdNET results is necessary for an efficient workflow when studying wolves
* Low-frequency, long-duration signals like wolf howls are intrinsically difficult for BirdNET to detect with high precision
* PAM combined with BirdNET can facilitate the fundamental task of assessing the distribution of wolves and/or coyotes across the landscape
Recommendations for Future Research:
* Prioritize for review BirdNET outputs with many wolf predictions recorded during likely periods of vocal activity for more effective wolf bioacoustics.
* Use the newly developed feature of BirdNET to train a custom detector to develop bespoke wolf detectors that can take advantage of project-specific training data.
* Explore interspecific interactions between wolves and coyotes using BirdNET to understand behavioral ecology.
* Facilitate estimates of group size of wolves and coyotes through efficient identification of their vocalizations.
* Use PAM to identify demographically critical events like successful reproduction by detecting distinctive pup sounds.
* Explore BirdNET's feature embeddings (accessible via the "embeddings.py" script) to gain further insights into wolf and coyote ecology and identify distinctive sounds.
* Undertake further work to apply BirdNET efficiently to wolf ecology given the challenges encountered.
* Incentivize further improvement to canid-oriented PAM techniques in general.
